slides.title: Nobody needs an orchestrator on day one. You *earn* one.
Orchestration multiplies
slides.body:
It doesn't create capability.
Reliable tasks → *leverage*.
Flaky tasks → an expensive way to run broken scripts in the right order.

slides.title: 1 — Tasks that are idempotent
slides.body:
Run it twice, same result.
If a second run makes anyone *nervous*, it isn't ready to run unattended at 2am.

slides.title: 2 — Data you actually trust
slides.body:
A stale source of truth doesn't slow the tool down.
It executes *confidently* against the wrong list.

slides.title: 3 — A rollback somebody has run
slides.body:
Executed, not documented.
*Half-applied* is the normal failure mode of orchestrated change.

slides.title: 4 — Failure you can see
slides.body:
"The job failed" isn't observability.
Which step? Which device? *In what state?*

slides.title: None of it needs a purchase order
slides.body: Just unglamorous work on what you already run — and it pays off *whether or not* a tool ever arrives.

slides.title: An orchestrator reveals how mature your automation already was.
slides.body:
It doesn't make it mature.
What's the one task you'd trust to run 500 times tonight, unattended?
